title: Azure grows 48% to $33 billion as Microsoft discloses the segment in dollars for the first time
subtitle: Microsoft Cloud topped $63 billion for the quarter and management guided Azure to 49–50% growth next quarter against capex of $45 billion — the first time the company has put a dollar figure on Azure revenue instead of only a percentage.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Microsoft reported fiscal Q1 2027 results — the quarter ending September 30 — after the close on October 28. Revenue rose 19% year over year to about $92.3 billion against a $90.7 billion consensus, and adjusted EPS was $4.89 against $4.73 expected. The headline for AI watchers: Azure revenue was $33.17 billion for the quarter, up 48% in constant currency, and Microsoft disclosed Azure revenue in dollars for the first time. The company has historically reported Azure as a growth rate only. Microsoft Cloud, the broader category that bundles Azure with other commercial cloud offerings, topped $63 billion for the quarter with growth accelerating to 30%. Commercial remaining performance obligations — the contracted backlog — surged 73% to $677 billion. Capital expenditures and finance leases were $45.2 billion, up about 30% year on year. Shares rose about 4% in extended trading.

The guidance is the part markets will trade on tomorrow. For fiscal Q2, Microsoft expects Azure revenue to grow 49–50% in constant currency — an acceleration from this quarter's 48% — against revenue guidance of $96.0–$97.1 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% year over year as capex ran at a quarterly pace that would annualize to roughly $180 billion, consistent with the roughly $170 billion the company has flagged for calendar 2026 and above the $190 billion range Microsoft had previously floated for the broader fiscal year. Management returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks during the quarter, and recently introduced a voluntary buyout scheme for around 60,000 employees, which signals a pivot toward higher spend on infrastructure and lower spend on headcount.

Moving Azure from a growth-rate-only disclosure to a dollar figure is a structural change in how AI cloud economics will be analyzed. For years, outsiders had to triangulate Azure's size from Intelligent Cloud segment math or Microsoft commentary. A $33 billion quarterly number — $133 billion annualized — now sits alongside Google Cloud's $30.7 billion quarter and Amazon's roughly $45–50 billion AWS run rate as a directly comparable line. Combined with Alphabet's 103% cloud growth reported the same evening (covered separately in today's digest), the night produced the first clean side-by-side read of hyperscaler AI monetization. The capex thesis gets its best defense of the year: Microsoft is spending at a $180-billion annual rate and growing the division consuming most of that capex nearly 50% in dollars.

A note for learners: when a company changes a disclosure, read the change itself. Microsoft had every incentive to keep Azure a percentage for as long as it could — percentages let a company shape the narrative without pinning down the base. The decision to put a dollar number on it now, under scrutiny about AI returns on investment, is a confidence signal: management thinks the dollar number helps them more than it hurts them. If you are learning to read financial statements, practice watching for these inflection points in disclosure practice. They often matter as much as the headline revenue number, because they tell you what the company thinks the question is about to be — and whether they feel ready to answer it.
